readerTitle: The integration worked. So why did nobody use it?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (레스토랑 예약 앱과 POS 회사의 연동, 호텔과 쿠킹 클래스) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 연동 파트너십은 기술이 아니라 파트너 회사 안에서 실제로 고객을 만나는 사람이 무엇으로 보상받는지에 따라 성패가 갈린다.
misconception: 두 회사 대표가 계약하고 연동이 잘 작동하면 고객은 자연히 따라온다. 수익 배분율만 높이면 파트너가 더 열심히 판다.

sources.text: SAL-07-03 (인센티브 정렬), SAL-07-04 (수익 배분) 레슨의 개념 적용

factChecks.note: 기존 조건 비교: 20% × $100 = 월 $20, 24개월 = $480, 이후에도 매달 $20씩 계속 지급. 새 조건이 24개월 기준으로도 $70 저렴하고 이후 비용은 0입니다.

cards.title: The integration worked. So why did nobody use it?
body: A small table-booking app signs a deal with a big point-of-sale company, the system restaurants use to take orders and payments. Bookings will flow straight into the till.
The engineers ship on time. The connection works perfectly. Six months later, almost no restaurants have turned it on.

image.label: Two puzzle pieces connected, gathering dust
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 레스토랑 카운터 위에 예약 태블릿과 POS 단말기가 퍼즐 조각처럼 완벽히 맞물려 있지만 위에 먼지가 쌓이고 거미줄이 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Each side wanted something different.
body: The booking app has 2,000 restaurants. The POS company has 40,000. The app wants access to them. The POS company wants a feature that keeps restaurants from switching to a rival till.
The deal: the POS company lists the app in its marketplace and mentions it to customers. In return, the app pays the POS company 20% of the monthly fee from every restaurant it refers. Forever.

cards.title: Why aren't the POS sales reps mentioning it?
body: The POS company's leaders love the partnership. But their sales reps, who visit restaurants every day, almost never bring it up. What's the most likely reason?

options.text: The reps were never trained on it
options.feedback: Training helps, and it's worth checking. But trained reps still skip things that don't help them hit their own targets.

options.text: The reps earn nothing from it, and it makes their sales calls longer
options.feedback: This is **aligning incentives** at work. The 20% goes to the company, not to the person in the room. For the rep, mentioning the app is extra work with no reward.

options.text: Restaurants don't actually want online booking
options.feedback: Possible, but you can't tell yet. If the people who pitch it aren't pitching it, low uptake says nothing about demand.

cards.title: A partnership runs on people, not logos.
body: Two CEOs signed the deal. But it lives or dies with the people who meet customers: sales reps, support staff, account managers.

Each of them already has targets and limited time. A partner's product gets attention only if helping it also helps them. **Aligning incentives** means checking what each person in the chain gets for doing what you need.

image.label: Chain from CEO to sales rep to restaurant, with one broken link
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽에서 오른쪽으로 "Your company → Partner CEO → Partner sales rep → Restaurant" 사슬. 영업 담당자 고리만 끊어져 있고 그 위에 "What's in it for me?" 말풍선.

cards.title: How should you rewrite the revenue share?
body: Each restaurant pays the app $100 a month and usually stays about two years. You get to propose new terms. Which works best?

options.text: Raise the company's share from 20% to 40%
options.feedback: You double your cost per customer, yet the reps still see nothing. More money to the wrong place doesn't change behavior.

options.text: 15% to the company for 24 months, plus $50 to the rep once a restaurant takes 30 bookings
options.feedback: **Sharing revenue** works best when it pays for the result you want. The rep is rewarded for real use, not a signup, and your cost has an end date.

options.text: Keep 20% forever, and add a $50 rep bonus for every signup
options.feedback: The rep now cares, which is progress. But paying per signup invites restaurants who never use it, and the forever share keeps costing you.

cards.title: What one referred restaurant costs you.
body: Over two years, a restaurant pays $2,400. The new terms cost **$410**, about 17%. The old terms cost $480 by then and kept going every month after.

breakdown.label: Left for you
breakdown.detail: And a rep who now brings it up

cards.callout: A smaller share, aimed at the right person, can buy more effort than a bigger one.

cards.title: People do exactly what you pay for.
body: Reward signups and you get signups, including restaurants that never use the product and cancel fast. Reward a long trial period and reps may push poor-fit customers.
So pick the trigger carefully. It should be close to the value both companies want, like real bookings taken. It should also be hard to fake. Check it after a few months and adjust.

cards.title: Now it's a hotel and a cooking school.
body: You run a cooking school. A nearby hotel agreed to recommend your classes, and you pay the hotel 10% of each booking. Three months in, almost no guests come. The front desk staff answer guest questions all day. What do you change?

options.feedback: The owner earns more, but the desk clerk talking to guests still gets nothing. You pay more for the same silence.

options.text: Give desk staff a small bonus per guest who attends, plus a simple booking card
options.feedback: This aligns incentives with the person who makes the recommendation, and pays on attendance, not a promise. The card makes saying yes easy.

options.text: Offer hotel guests a 15% discount code
options.feedback: It makes the offer more attractive once guests hear about it. But if staff don't mention it, few guests ever will.

cards.title: Pay the person in the room, for the result you want.
body: Concepts used: **Aligning incentives** (who inside the partner gets rewarded) and **Sharing revenue** (paying for real use, with an end date).
**Try it today:** pick one partner. Name the person who actually talks to customers about you. Write down what they gain when they do.
